1.pericope_label: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Jews which dwell in the land of Egypt: ye have seen all the evil that I have brought upon Jerusalem
debates: Where Pathros lay
How long after the arrival in Egypt the discourse was delivered
Whether Migdol is the fortress of the older books or a later settlement
outliers: Ellicott reports that Lepsius distinguishes the Migdol of this verse from the older fortress and identifies it with the camp which Herodotus says Psammetichus founded for his mercenaries
Clarke reports Dahler as placing the discourse in the seventeenth or eighteenth year after the taking of Jerusalem, where Ellicott says there is no certain note of the interval
Calvin observes that the word was directly given to Jeremiah alone, God not favouring the Jews with the honour of speaking to them but sending the Prophet as his messenger
themes: A people scattered over the principal parts of a foreign country
A festival used as the occasion for a warning
Fools who are beaten and do not become wise
Upstart deities whose origin was not worth noticing

4.pericope_label: Howbeit I sent unto you all my servants the prophets, rising early and sending them: but they hearkened not, nor inclined their ear
debates: What kind of language the rising early describes
Whether the word abominable is a general or a specialised term
What the great evil against their souls is
outliers: Clarke calls the entreaty one of the finest figures of poetry when judiciously managed, the ascribing of human passions to God, and lists grief, mourning, compassion, repentance and anger among its instances
Calvin observes that the law needs only two or three witnesses to condemn, whereas a whole succession of prophets had been sent, so that the people were convicted by a great number
Calvin insists that God receives no loss from their wickedness, since nothing is taken from his greatness when men rob him of worship, and they become only the authors of their own destruction
themes: A commandment softened into an entreaty
Prophets sent one after another as witnesses
Ears deliberately closed rather than merely inattentive
Wrath poured out like something molten

9.pericope_label: Have ye forgotten the wickedness of your fathers, and the wickedness of their wives? they are not humbled even unto this day
debates: Whether the wickedness mentioned means their sins or their punishments
Who the few that escape are
Whether the limiting clause at the end of the passage is original
outliers: Ellicott reports that some critics have looked on the clause about those who escape as an interpolation, inserted to bring the verse into agreement with a later one
Calvin offers two ways of reconciling the verse with itself, either that the few preserved are those carried into Egypt against their will, or that the end of the verse looks to the exiles in Babylon
Clarke and Ellicott both make the women the chief agents of the idolatry, the queens burning incense to the queen of heaven and their example followed by the wives of the nobles
themes: Wives named among the wicked alongside kings
A people broken and still not humbled
A nation used as the form of an oath
Exiles still lifting up their souls to return

15.pericope_label: Then all the men which knew that their wives had burned incense unto other gods answered Jeremiah: we will not hearken unto thee
debates: Whether the husbands knew of the idolatry of their wives
Whether the refusal denies that the message came from God or defies it
Where superstition begins
outliers: Wesley holds that the women did it with some privacy, so that all their husbands did not know of it, where Gill and Henry say the husbands knew and winked at it
Calvin makes the wilfulness of men the fountain of all superstitions, so that religion remains pure only by adopting nothing but what God prescribes
Ellicott sets the arrangement beside the practice of imperial Rome, where the women kept a worship in which their husbands acquiesced without joining
themes: Men indifferent enough to let their wives worship anything
Guilt that makes reproof intolerable
A prophet proved by the calamities he foretold
Men making themselves legislators in the worship of God

18.pericope_label: But since we left off to burn incense to the queen of heaven, we have wanted all things: did we make her cakes without our men?
debates: Whether the speakers in the nineteenth verse are the women or the men
When, if ever, the people left off the worship
Why the calamities followed
outliers: Calvin denies that the women are the speakers in the nineteenth verse, since the masculine gender is used and the context shows men are meant, and takes the clause as an appeal to the consent of a whole people
Gill reports Kimchi as holding that they never ceased from the worship at all, but said whenever evil came that it was because they had ceased or slackened
Ellicott compares the argument with the one the Romans used when calamities fell on the Empire, that they suffered because they had left off the old worship
themes: Prosperity remembered and its cause mistaken
Cakes shaped like a crescent
Sins that left the sinner rather than the sinner his sins
A boast admitted and then turned round

21.pericope_label: The incense that ye burned in the cities of Judah, did not the Lord remember them? so that the Lord could no longer bear
debates: Why incense in particular is named
What the forbearance of God shows
Whether the Law alone would have sufficed without the prophets
outliers: Calvin argues from two principles, that God is not angry without reason and that he was always propitious even to the unworthy seed of Abraham, so that the atrocity of the punishment shows the atrocity of the sin
Calvin holds that the naming of incense is a part put for the whole, covering all false and corrupt modes of worship
Keil and Delitzsch call the twenty-third verse an emphatic and brief repetition of what has already been said, and note a variant form of one word in it
themes: A calamity traced back past chance to a decree
Peace and plenty enjoyed during a delay mistaken for approval
A part named to stand for a whole worship
Vows kept that ought to have been broken

26.pericope_label: Behold, I have sworn by my great name: I will watch over them for evil, and not for good
debates: Why God confirms a threatening with an oath
How the promise that a few shall escape agrees with the earlier word that none should
What kind of sign is meant
outliers: Calvin distinguishes signs that precede an event, like the fleece of Gideon, from signs coincident with it, like the word to Moses about sacrificing in the mountain, and puts this one in the second class
Calvin holds that those who escape cease to be counted among the residue, having separated themselves, so that there would be Jews no more in Egypt
Gill names Jeremiah and Baruch among the few who escape, on the authority of two Jewish commentators
themes: An oath used because plain speech had failed
A watchfulness that is dreadful rather than comforting
A remnant that leaves off being a remnant
A sign that only proves itself afterwards

30.pericope_label: Behold, I will give Pharaoh-hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies, as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar
debates: What the surname of the king means
How the prophecy was fulfilled
Why a sign was needed at all
outliers: Calvin admits he does not know the meaning of the surname, thinking it probably an Egyptic word since there is none such in Hebrew, and adds that it is not known whence the word Pharaoh itself has come
Clarke follows the ancient historians in tracing the fall of the king to the revolt of his own subjects under Amasis, whom they proclaimed king while he was still speaking to them
Calvin notes that the Jews thought Egypt unassailable, especially from the side of Pelusium, so that they reckoned themselves beyond the reach of danger
themes: A royal title borne like the name of a Caesar
A general crowned in the middle of his own speech
A sign left buried until its time
Confidence in a fortress laughed to scorn
